teaser: A man who demanded thousands of executions, painted as gently as a sleeping saint.

lesson.text: Something in this picture does not add up. A man has just been stabbed in the chest, and yet nothing here is violent. No struggle, no scream, no killer. His face is close to a smile. The scene is a murder, but it is painted like a lullaby.

The man is Jean-Paul Marat, and in life he was anything but gentle. A journalist of the French Revolution, he used his newspaper to call for the heads of the Revolution's enemies, by the hundreds and then the thousands. Many Parisians adored him. Many others were terrified of him.

On July 13, 1793, a 24-year-old woman from Normandy named Charlotte Corday talked her way into his apartment. Marat suffered from a painful skin disease and worked for hours in a medicinal bath. She found him there, and killed him with a kitchen knife she had bought that morning.

Jacques-Louis David knew that room. He was Marat's political ally, an elected deputy as well as France's most famous painter, and by his own account he had visited Marat the day before the murder and found him writing in his tub.

The very next day, a fellow deputy called on David in the assembly to paint Marat. He also staged the funeral. What he delivered that autumn is one of the first great political images of modern times, and its method is simple: keep what serves the hero, remove everything else.

lesson.title: What David kept
lesson.text: The body tells one story. Follow it from the head down to the floor.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Head wrapped in a white cloth, eyes closed, lips slightly parted. Marat's skin was badly damaged by his illness. David paints it smooth and golden, like wax or marble.

spots.title: The wound
spots.text: A short, clean cut below the collarbone, with a thin line of blood. It is small enough to miss. The bathwater and the sheet beside it carry the red instead.

spots.title: The pen
spots.text: The arm hangs to the floor, and the fingers still hold a quill. David's Marat dies in the middle of a sentence. For a writer, there is no nobler way to be found.

spots.title: The knife
spots.text: In the darkest corner, a blade with a pale handle and blood on the steel. In reality the knife stayed in the wound. David moves it to the floor so the body stays clean.

lesson.text: That hanging arm had a long history. Painters and sculptors had used it for centuries for one body in particular: the dead Christ, taken down from the cross. David, who studied in Rome, knew those works by heart. He lends their pose to a politician.
Two lines hold the whole composition, and a third thing is missing.

lines.label: The fall
lines.text: From the tilted head, down the shoulder and along the arm to the floor: one slow, slumping curve. This is the line borrowed from images of the dead Christ.

lines.label: The board
lines.text: A plank covered in green cloth cuts straight across. It hides the tub and the water, and it turns a bath into something closer to a desk, or a tomb.

lines.label: Nothing
lines.text: Almost half the canvas is empty: brown-green paint, loosely brushed, lighter toward the right. The real room had wallpaper and objects on the wall. David replaced them with silence.

lesson.text: David does not lie about the death. He edits it. Every removed detail, the killer, the mess, the wallpaper, pushes the scene away from a crime report and toward an altarpiece.

Then come the papers, and here the painting starts to argue. Marat cannot speak for himself anymore, so David lets handwriting do it. There are two notes in the picture, and they are meant to be compared.
Marat's left hand holds a letter. Whose name can you read on it?

spots.title: Corday's letter
spots.text: Dated July 13, 1793, from Marie Anne Charlotte Corday “to citizen Marat.” It says her unhappiness gives her a right to his kindness. She is never shown, but the painting convicts her: she used his pity to reach him.

lesson.text: The second note lies on the wooden crate, under a banknote of the Revolution. It is in Marat's hand, and it orders that the money be given to a mother of five whose husband died for his country. One paper shows a trap. The other shows a last act of charity.
The makeshift desk is true to life. Marat really did write on an upturned wooden box next to his bath. His actual bathtub, shaped like a tall boot, still exists and is kept in a Paris wax museum.

On the front of that crate, David paints letters as if carved in stone: “À MARAT, DAVID.” To Marat, from David. Below, in small script, “l'an deux,” Year Two, the date in the new calendar that began with the Republic. A packing box has become a gravestone.

The painting was presented to the national assembly in November 1793 and copied for display around the country. Its glory lasted months. In July 1794 the radical government fell. Marat went from martyr to monster, and David went to prison.

The canvas was handed back to David in 1795 and kept out of sight for decades. Exiled after Napoleon's fall, he ended his life in Brussels, which is why France's most famous revolutionary painting hangs today in Belgium.

The poet Charles Baudelaire saw it in 1846 and was shaken by its tenderness. He understood that it works on you whether or not you approve of the man in the bath. That is the unsettling part. The picture is honest about the pen and the wound, and silent about everything Marat wrote with that pen.

So go back to the calm that seemed wrong at the start. It was never a mistake. It is the argument. How much of what you feel in front of an image comes from what happened, and how much from the way someone chose to show it?

quiz.question: Why was Marat in a bath when he was killed?
options: He was hiding from the police
He soaked for hours to relieve a skin disease
It was a hot summer day
quiz.explanation: He worked in a medicinal bath because of a painful skin condition.

quiz.question: What did David change about the knife?
options: He moved it from the wound to the floor
He put it in Marat's hand
quiz.explanation: The knife stayed in the wound in reality; David placed it on the floor.

quiz.question: The hanging arm echoes older images of whom?
quiz.explanation: The pose was long used for Christ taken down from the cross.

quiz.question: What does the note on the crate say Marat was doing?
options: Sending money to a war widow with five children
quiz.explanation: The note orders that the banknote be given to a mother of five whose husband died for the country.

quiz.question: Why is the painting in Brussels today?
options: David lived there in exile at the end of his life
Belgium bought it at auction in 1793
Napoleon gave it to the city
quiz.explanation: David was exiled after Napoleon's fall and died in Brussels.

facts.text: Charlotte Corday appears in the shadows at the right of the painting.
facts.explanation: She is never shown; only her name appears on the letter.

facts.text: David was a politician as well as a painter, and an ally of Marat.
facts.explanation: He was an elected deputy and Marat's political ally.

facts.text: The upper half of the canvas shows the wallpaper of Marat's real bathroom.
facts.explanation: David replaced the real decor with an empty, loosely brushed background.
